results.name: upward_minus_downward_extrapolation
results.description: Yes rate on targets 1-15 above the largest example minus yes rate on targets 1-15 below the smallest example (sets of 2+ examples); observed above null means people extend ranges upward more (or downward less) than the model's symmetric interval/rule account predicts.
results.code:
# name: upward_minus_downward_extrapolation
# description: Yes rate on targets 1-15 above the largest example minus yes rate on targets 1-15 below the smallest example (sets of 2+ examples); observed above null means people extend ranges upward more (or downward less) than the model's symmetric interval/rule account predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).values
    t = df["target"].astype(float).values
    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(axis=1)
    mx, mn = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1), np.nanmin(ex, axis=1)
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    up = (n >= 2) & (t > mx) & (t <= mx + 15)
    dn = (n >= 2) & (t < mn) & (t >= mn - 15)
    if up.sum() == 0 or dn.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[up].mean() - r[dn].mean())

results.name: single_example_generalization_rate
results.description: Yes rate on non-example targets for sets with exactly one example; observed above null means the model under-generalises from a single example (too narrow), below means it over-generalises.

results.name: decade_share_effect_near
results.description: Among non-example targets 1-10 away from the nearest example, yes rate when the target shares a tens digit (decade) with some example minus when it does not; observed above null means people give extra yes for a shared decade that the model lacks, below means the model over-predicts decade sharing.
results.code:
# name: decade_share_effect_near
# description: Among non-example targets 1-10 away from the nearest example, yes rate when the target shares a tens digit (decade) with some example minus when it does not; observed above null means people give extra yes for a shared decade that the model lacks, below means the model over-predicts decade sharing.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).values
    t = df["target"].astype(float).values
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    dec = (np.floor(ex / 10) == np.floor(t / 10)[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    near = (dist >= 1) & (dist <= 10)
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    a, b = near & dec, near & ~dec
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: near_minus_far_distance_gradient
results.description: Yes rate on non-example targets within 10 of the nearest example minus yes rate on targets more than 20 from every example; observed above null means people show a steeper numerical-proximity gradient than the model, below means the model's similarity gradient is too steep.
results.code:
# name: near_minus_far_distance_gradient
# description: Yes rate on non-example targets within 10 of the nearest example minus yes rate on targets more than 20 from every example; observed above null means people show a steeper numerical-proximity gradient than the model, below means the model's similarity gradient is too steep.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).values
    t = df["target"].astype(float).values
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    a, b = (dist >= 1) & (dist <= 10), dist > 20
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: partial_final_digit_match_rate
results.description: In sets whose examples do NOT all share one final digit, yes rate on non-example targets whose final digit matches at least one example's; observed above null means people use loose final-digit similarity that the model's all-or-none "ends in d" rules miss, below means the model over-credits it.
results.code:
# name: partial_final_digit_match_rate
# description: In sets whose examples do NOT all share one final digit, yes rate on non-example targets whose final digit matches at least one example's; observed above null means people use loose final-digit similarity that the model's all-or-none "ends in d" rules miss, below means the model over-credits it.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    exi = np.nan_to_num(ex, nan=-1).astype(int)
    ones = np.where(valid, exi % 10, -1)
    first = ones[:, 0]
    all_same = ((ones == first[:, None]) | ~valid).all(axis=1)
    match = ((ones == (t % 10)[:, None]) & valid).any(axis=1)
    in_set = (exi == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    m = ~all_same & match & ~in_set
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].values[m].mean())

results.name: common_digit_containment_yes_rate
results.description: For sets of 2+ examples in which some digit appears in every example, yes rate on non-example targets that contain that digit but do not share any example's final digit; observed above null means people generalise "contains digit d" more than the model (which has no such concepts), below means less.
results.code:
# name: common_digit_containment_yes_rate
# description: For sets of 2+ examples in which some digit appears in every example, yes rate on non-example targets that contain that digit but do not share any example's final digit; observed above null means people generalise "contains digit d" more than the model (which has no such concepts), below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(axis=1)
    exi = np.nan_to_num(ex, nan=-1).astype(int)
    valid = exi >= 0
    tens, ones = exi // 10, exi % 10
    hit = np.zeros(len(df), dtype=bool)
    for d in range(10):
        has = ((ones == d) | ((tens % 10 == d) & (exi >= 10)) | ((exi == 100) & (d in (0, 1)))) | ~valid
        common = has.all(axis=1) & (n >= 2)
        tcont = (t % 10 == d) | ((t // 10 % 10 == d) & (t >= 10)) | ((t == 100) & (d in (0, 1)))
        hit |= common & tcont
    same_final = ((ones == (t % 10)[:, None]) & valid).any(axis=1)
    in_set = (exi == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    m = hit & ~same_final & ~in_set
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].values[m].mean())

results.name: example_target_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate on trials whose target is itself one of the shown examples; observed above null means the model under-endorses the examples themselves (too much noise/outside-concept mass), below means it over-endorses them.

results.name: late_minus_early_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate on trials in the last third of the session (trial_index >= 300) minus the first third (trial_index < 150); nonzero observed vs a near-zero null means a drift in willingness to say yes over the session that the stationary model cannot produce (positive = people become more liberal over time).
